paper_title: Iris-Z: Scaling One Generative Model Past Specialist Geometry Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified model: a single generative model with a single generative training task that handles all of them within the same backbone, and keeps improving with data, parameters and compute. We believe the bitter lesson applies just as much to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, in the end to visual intelligence: the effort should go into general architectures that solve all these tasks in a unified way, and into scaling them, rather than into task-specific designs. We test this on monocular geometry, a task that has belonged to specialised architectures for years. Iris-Z is a general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together. A single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands the image and its depth at the same time, and one set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto a given depth. At enough scale it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists on established depth benchmarks while keeping the generative abilities of the backbone it started from without specialized layers. We release two models for the community.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: speridlabs P T H A P 2 0 2 6 R A E R E A T E PAT I L E Iris-Z: Scaling One Generative Model Past Specialist Geometry Models Alejandro Cañada, Chema Garabito SperidLabs Project lead Code and models: github.com/speridlabs/iris-z-sdk T T Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified model: single generative model with single generative training task that handles all of them within the same backbone, and keeps improving with data, parameters and compute. We believe the bitter lesson applies just as much to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, in the end to visual intelligence: the effort should go into general architectures that solve all these tasks in unified way, and into scaling them, rather than into task-specific designs. We test this on monocular geometry, task that has belonged to specialised architectures for years. Iris-Z is general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together. single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands the image and its depth at the same time, and one set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto given depth. At enough scale it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists on established depth benchmarks while keeping the generative abilities of the backbone it started from without specialized layers. We release two models for the community. . 1 Top: prompt image and depth, generated together. Bottom: photographs depth. All from Iris-Z-big. Depth is coloured on log distance, near = red, far = blue; black: no depth or sky. P T 2 0 2 6 R A E R R - C C E T 1 01 Introduction Language went from many task-specific models to one unified model that handles all of them within the same backbone: single generative model with single generative training task, simple and foundational enough to cover all the others. Trained to predict the next token on enough data, it learned to translate, summarise and answer questions at level competitive with models built for each of those tasks [1]. And the same single model kept getting better at every one of those tasks as data, parameters and compute grew [2, 3], giving one way to scale every text task forward at once. We believe this is the bitter lesson in its plainest form: general methods that scale with computation end up ahead of task-specific methods [4]. We believe the bitter lesson applies to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, and in the end to visual intelligence, as much as it applied to language. The effort should go into finding general architectures that solve all of these fields and tasks in unified way, and then into scaling that one model as far as possible, rather than into task-specific designs. Visual intelligence is now following this path through visual generative models. For example, Vision Banana instruction-tunes the Nano Banana Pro image generator on small amount of task data and matches or beats specialists such as Segment Anything 3 and Depth Anything without losing its ability to generate [6]. Veo 3 segments objects, finds edges and solves simple visual tasks without being trained for any of them [5]. Models trained to both understand and generate images with the same weights such as BAGEL [7] and PixelUMM [8] also point in similar direction. Data is the other half of this argument. General generative models can be trained on massive amounts of visual data, web-scale images and videos that need no labels designed for one task. unified architecture such as Iris-Z, where each modality is one more group of tokens in the same sequence, lets more modalities join that training. In our experiments, the larger the pre-trained generator and the more data it is trained on, the better it does on task-specific benchmarks (Fig. 2b): parameter count, compute and above all scalable pre-training data are what move the result. The more compute and data go into single architecture, the better it becomes at each specific task, which gives one way to scale every visual task at once. Monocular geometry is hard place to test this. The reference model, MoGe-3 [11], is task-specific ViT that as of today leads the benchmarks. In MoGe-3s own comparison, models like Apples Depth Pro [12], ByteDances Depth Anything 3 [13], UniDepth V2 or UniK3D all stay behind it. Image generators that are repurposed as depth estimators like the Marigold family [14, 16], although strong, still perform worse than MoGe-3 and also than MoGe-2 when evaluated on MoGe-3s held-out test sets. Vision Banana reports lower metric-depth error than MoGe-2 [10], but it predates MoGe-3 and is not available to test. We built Iris-Z to test this idea and to show that general model can beat models designed for one task. We took general image generator and taught it not only to generate appearance (RGB) but to generate and reason about geometry (depth) jointly with it, denoising both together as one RGBD output. In Iris-Z appearance and geometry are produced together, and single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands both at once. Our view is that generative model should generate and understand the world in all its modalities jointly, and that the geometry it produces along with an image is part of what it knows about the scene and the world. We see this as path forward to unifying visual understanding. The same recipe extends to further modalities, such as surface normals, segmentation, motion or the camera, each added as one more group of tokens in the same sequence, so that single model learns all of them together and improves on all of them as it scales. In our experiments generalist image models have proven better than specialists with enough scale. IrisZ-big is, to our knowledge, the first open generalpurpose generator to beat MoGe-3 on Marigolds benchmarks, and it is also ahead of MoGe-3 on average on MoGe-3s own benchmarks at the resolutions it was trained for, while still being general generative model that does the same tasks it did before we re-trained it. Each step of scale we added, more data, full fine-tune and larger backbone, improved the result (Fig. 2b) without the need for depth-specific layer. We take this as sign that generative AI, computer vision and spatial intelligence are converging on one model that has all of these capabilities and scales better than todays specialised systems. In summary, we make the following contributions: Iris-Z, generative model that denoises image and depth jointly in one sequence and serves four tasks with one set of weights, released in two sizes, IrisZ-big and Iris-Z-small. State-of-the-art affine-invariant depth performance on Marigolds and MoGe-3s benchmarks (Sec. 6). Evidence that the improvement in depth estimation comes from scale rather than task design. Across E N 2 0 2 6 R A E R R - C C E T 2 three runs we changed only the training data and the backbone size, and each run lowers the depth error (Sec. 6). . 2 Iris-Z on Marigold V2s benchmarks, mean AbsRel100 (lower is better). a: Our two models vs Marigold V2 and MoGe-3. b: scaling: LoRA on Iris-Z-smalls backbone that saw 0.2M frames, full fine-tune of it (Iris-Z-small) that saw 3.8M unique frames, then Iris-Zbig, backbone 3.5 larger, that saw 3.6M. Black: 40 inference passes, the sampler we report; grey: 10 passes. c: accuracy against the number of DiT passes per image (4: one seed, 10: 2 steps from 5 seeds, 40: 4 steps from 10 seeds). Iris-Z-bigs 10-pass points are from an earlier checkpoint of the same training. 02 Related Work Monocular depth specialists. Learning depth from single image began with networks regressed on one dataset at time, with scale-invariant loss to deal with the ambiguity of single view [23]. MiDaS showed that mixing many datasets with different scales trained with loss invariant to scale and shift transferred to unseen domains far better than any single source [24]. DPT moved the same recipe to vision transformer [25]. Metric depth needed camera-aware approaches like ZoeDepth which adds metric heads to relative model [26], Metric3D that maps every image to canonical camera [27] or UniDepth that predicts the camera together with the depth [28]. Depth Anything scaled the training data instead, pseudo-labelling about 62M unlabelled images with teacher [29]; its second version trains that teacher on synthetic data only [30]. Depth Pro then focused on sharp boundaries and focal length estimation [12], and Depth Anything 3 extended the approach to multiple views [13]. MoGe predicts an affine-invariant point map with robust alignment in training [9], MoGe-2 adds metric scale [10], and MoGe-3 refines the point map in 3D with sparse convolutions [11]. This line of work improved by finding better depth-specific strategies and more varied and better labelled data, while each model stayed taskspecific. Generative priors for dense prediction. Marigold showed that text-to-image latent diffusion model fine-tuned on small amount of synthetic data becomes strong zero-shot depth estimator [14]. Much of the follow-up work made this faster: DepthFM replaces diffusion with flow matching from image to depth [32], Lotus predicts the clean target in single step [33], and Martin Garcia et al. show that singlestep model matches the multi-step one [15]. Other work extended it to new outputs and backbones. GeoWizard predicts depth and normals together [31], DepthCrafter applies the approach to video generator [34], Marigold V2 moves to diffusion transformers [16], and Iris-3B compares pixel and latent-space generators [17]. In all of these the generator becomes an image-to-depth model. The image is always the input, and the ability to generate images is lost along the way. Iris-Z keeps the generative objective and textto-image generation, and depth estimation is one of several tasks the same joint model performs. Joint RGB-D and multi-modal generation. smaller line of work produces geometry together with appearance. LDM3D trains one latent diffusion model to output an image and its depth from prompt [35], while JointNet keeps the text-to-image model frozen and adds parallel branch for dense modality such as depth [36]. Wonder3D extends this across views, producing colours and normals with cross-domain attention [37], and Aether trains video model to predict geometry alongside the frames [38]. None of these were shown to reach specialist accuracy on established depth benchmarks, which is the gap Iris-Z addresses. Generalist vision through generation. Visual incontext learning shows model an example input and its output side by side together with new input, and asks it to fill in the missing output, so the task is defined by the example rather than by the architecture. P T 2 0 2 6 R A E R I - C C E T 3 Bar et al. do this with an inpainting model on grid of images [39], and Painter trains masked image model on many tasks in this format [40]. InstructCV instruction-tunes text-to-image model to perform vision tasks named in text [41], and OmniGen trains one generator for editing, conditional generation and several classic vision tasks [42]. More recently, Vision Banana showed that frontier image generator with instruction-tuning matches specialists on segmentation and depth [6], and Veo 3 solves visual tasks it was never trained for [5]. Unified multimodal models go further and both read and write images in one network. Transfusion combines next-token prediction and diffusion in one transformer [43], Janus uses separate visual encoders for understanding and generation [44], and BAGEL and PixelUMM train such models at larger scale [7, 8]. Scaling visual generators. Diffusion transformers improve predictably with compute [45], and rectifiedflow transformers show smooth scaling of validation loss that tracks human preference up to billions of parameters [46]. Whether the geometry generator learns scales the same way is less studied. Our scaling path (Fig. 2b) is first data point for the depth modality. 03 Method Iris-Z comes from pretrained text-to-image diffusion transformer and the only new parameters we add belong to learned modality embedding. There is no depth head and no second network. Depth is encoded as an image by the same autoencoder that encodes the image and placed in the same token sequence, and training uses the base models flow-matching loss together with loss on the decoded depth. Below we describe how image and depth share one sequence  (Fig. 3)  , how depth is represented, which tasks are trained, and how we sample. The backbones, training settings and data are in Sec. 4. Image and depth in one sequence. The image and its depth are both encoded as images by the backbones autoencoder, and their latents form one token sequence together with the prompt. Each token carries three embeddings that identify it. The spatial position embedding (the backbones rotary row and column) is the same for the image token and the depth token of patch, so the model knows they describe the same point of the scene. The sequence position embedding, an extra rotary coordinate the backbone already uses to tell several input images apart, is 0 for image tokens and 1 for depth tokens. learned modality embedding labels each token as generated image, generated depth, given image or given depth. Image and depth each carry their own flow-matching time t: whichever is generated follows the rectifiedflow objective of the base model [20, 46] at its own t, and whichever is given is fed clean and modulated with = 0. Because attention runs over the whole sequence, image and depth condition each other at every step of denoising. Depth as an image. Depth is stored as per-image normalised log ray distance. The 2nd to 98th percentile of an images log distance is mapped to [1, 0.95], so every image uses the same range and the prediction is defined up to scale and shift in log space. Sky is set to +1, which leaves margin between the farthest real depth and the sky. The value is copied into three channels and encoded by the same autoencoder as the image, without changes; decoding averages the three channels. At inference, pixels above 0.975 are marked as sky. Do multiple tasks with the same weights. Each training sample draws one task. Joint: image and depth are noised to the same time and both are scored (prompt RGBD). Image given: only depth is denoised (image depth). Depth given: the reverse (depth image). Independent: image and depth are noised to independent times. Image only: the depth stays pure noise and only the image is scored (prompt image); this keeps training plain text-to-image generation and prevents the model from drifting away from the base models images. With this mix of tasks, one set of weights serves four tasks at inference. second loss decodes the depth the model currently predicts and compares it with the target in pixel space. Captions are dropped for share of samples, so image depth works without prompt. P T 2 0 2 6 R A E R R - C C E T 4 . 3 Iris-Z. The prompt, the image and the depth are encoded into one token sequence and processed by single DiT. Image and depth share the VAE encoder and decoder. Image and depth enter as noisy latents, or clean when the task gives them. Sampling depth. Image depth denoises the depth with the image given and an empty prompt, so both branches of classifier-free guidance are identical and each step costs one transformer pass. Sampling starts from noise, so we combine few short trajectories from different seeds (Sec. 4.4). 04 Implementation Details

sections.title: 4.1 Backbones
sections.content: We use two open text-to-image transformers from the FLUX.2 family as the backbone [18, 19]: Iris-Zbig starts from FLUX.2 [dev] (32B parameters, Mistral Small 24B text encoder) and Iris-Z-small from FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B (Qwen3-8B text encoder). Both are full fine-tunes of the transformer; the autoencoder and the text encoder stay frozen. FLUX.2 [dev] is guidance-distilled: we remove its guidance embedding and train classifier-free guidance back through caption dropout. The only new parameters are the modality embedding, initialised at zero, so training starts from the unchanged base model.

sections.title: 4.2 Training
sections.content: Both models are trained with AdamW in bf16 mixed precision and with sharded data parallelism. The decoded-depth loss takes the clean depth latent implied by the prediction, ˆx0 = xt v, decodes it with the frozen autoencoder and computes an L1 to the target over valid pixels, weighted by (1 t) so that near-clean steps count most; it is added with weight 1 to the flow-matching loss of every sample whose depth is scored. On sources with sparse or holed depth (LiDAR, stereo, relative reconstructions) only this decoded loss supervises depth, on measured pixels. Iris-Z-big keeps headroom for sky: real depth is squeezed into [1, 0.95] and sky alone is +1; Iris-Zsmall uses the full range. We keep two exponential moving averages of the weights; the slower one is better on every benchmark for both models and is the one we release. Iris-Z-big trains at constant learning rate and is then annealed linearly to zero over its last 750 steps; IrisZ-small keeps constant learning rate. Both start at about 5122 pixels and move growing share of samples to about 10242, ending at 42% (Iris-Z-big) and 56% (Iris-Z-small).

sections.title: 4.3 Data
sections.content: Each model was trained on about 3 to 4 million unique RGB-D frames, drawn from pool of real indoor captures, driving scenes with LiDAR and stereo, multiview reconstructions, rendered scenes and generated images. Every source was converted to metric ray distance. Sensor holes and sparse LiDAR stay as holes: on those frames depth is supervised only on measured pixels. Sky follows one rule per source and is stored as fixed far value. Every frame has dense caption, used as the prompt. Iris-Z-small saw about 3.8M unique frames, Iris-Z-big about 3.6M. Images are stored at about 5122 and 10242 pixels. Validation frames are held out per source, split by scene. We do not train on the benchmark datasets.

sections.title: 4.4 Sampling and generation
sections.content: Image depth runs 4 steps from each of 10 seeds. Each seeds prediction is the average of the cleandepth estimates ˆx0 = xt from its last two steps. The seeds are aligned to reference by least-squares scale and shift in log space and reduced by the perpixel median: 40 transformer passes per image. Images under 0.5 MP run at about 5122 pixels, larger P T 2 0 2 6 R A E R R - C C E T 5 ones at about 10242 (with one exception on MoGe-3s benchmarks, Sec. 5). The benchmark then fits its own alignment to the result, as for any model. Prompt image and prompt RGBD use 50 steps with classifier-free guidance (3.5 for Iris-Z-big, 4.0 for Iris-Z-small). For prompt RGBD the depth of the joint generation can be used as is, or re-estimated from the finished image with the image depth sampler, which is sharper. Depth image denoises the image with the depth given clean, starting from Gaussian noise: 50 steps from one seed with classifier-free guidance between the caption and the empty prompt. Without prompt there is no guidance and each step is one transformer pass. Holes in the given depth are filled with the nearest measured value.

sections.title: 4.5 Generation is preserved
sections.content: A depth estimator that forgets how to draw would be just another specialist. We generate with fixed heldout prompts and seeds and compare with the untouched base model on the same prompts and seeds (Tab. 1, Fig. 4) to ensure that Iris-Z is in fact general model. Prompt adherence holds as CLIP stays within 0.4 of the base model, slightly above it for Iris-Z-small. Images keep the base models subject and composition (similarity 0.880.89). Preference scores drop (HPSv2.1 24.3 against 26.7 for Iris-Z-big) as the models drift little towards the look of their training data. That same drift makes Iris-Z-bigs images more photographic (0.48 against 0.38). . 1 Prompt image against the untouched base model, same prompts and seeds, 50 steps with guidance. Bottom: Iris-Z, the image from joint RGBD generation. 05 Evaluation Benchmarks. Two tables, each run exactly as its paper defines it. Marigolds: NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet and DIODE with Marigold V2s split lists and masks (3,331 images), scored after RANSAC scale-and-shift alignment in log depth. MoGe-3s: NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, iBims-1, Sintel, DIODE and HAMMER with MoGes masks (4,470 images), scored after MoGes relative-error L1 alignment. We report AbsRel100. Sets and resolution. We leave out two of MoGe3s nine sets, Spring (2 MP) and Synth4K (8 MP): both models were trained at up to about 10242 pixels, and these sets test resolutions we did not train for. ETH3D, also high resolution, stays because it is one of Marigold V2s benchmarks too. On Marigolds table we keep the rule of Sec. 4.4 (under 0.5 MP at about 5122, larger at about 10242). On MoGe-3s table, sets with sparse LiDAR ground truth (KITTI) also run at about 10242. Baselines. Marigold V2 (a single-step model by design, one pass) and MoGe-3 (ViT-G, resolution level 9, 3 refinement steps) are run by our code on the same pixels. 06 Results MoGe-3s protocol. On MoGe-3s own benchmarks and alignment (Tab. 3, Fig. 5) Iris-Z-big is the most accurate model on average (3.56 against 3.70 for MoGe3) and on six of the seven sets; MoGe-3 keeps DIODE. Iris-Z-small is ahead of MoGe-3 on NYUv2 and HAMMER and behind on average (3.84). Marigolds protocol. Iris-Z-big is the most accurate model on Marigolds benchmarks (Tab. 4): 2.92, against 3.12 for MoGe-3 and 4.10 for Marigold V2. It is best on NYUv2, ETH3D and ScanNet; MoGe-3 keeps KITTI and DIODE. Iris-Z-small, at 9B, is level with MoGe-3 (3.11). Note that the estimates on the datasets that appear in both protocols (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, DIODE) differ because each protocol prepares the data differently: Marigolds uses the native images and cameras with fixed depth ranges and crops, while MoGes rerenders every sample into centred, undistorted pinhole view (cropping or zooming some sets). P T 2 0 2 6 R A E R R - C C E T 6 (Iris-Z-big at an earlier checkpoint). The larger backbone is better on both tables. Nothing about depth changed between these runs. Cost. Tab. 2 sets accuracy against cost. One step of Iris-Z-big takes 0.35 at 5122 and 1.4 at 10242 on one H200, so one prediction (40 passes) takes about 15 at 5122; Iris-Z-small takes 0.10 per step and 4.8 per prediction. specialist is still much cheaper per image: MoGe-3 takes 0.41 at 5122 on the same GPU (0.06 of it for its 3 refinement steps), about 37 times less. Iris-Z-big 1.90 1.76 2.25 4.16 4. 2.92 07 Discussion Towards one model. We did not set out to build better depth estimator. We wanted to know whether model that only knew RGB could learn the geometry of what it paints, without giving anything up. It could. With no depth head and no new architecture, only one extra embedding, Iris-Z-big now beats MoGe-3, model built for this one job, on the resolutions we trained on, and it still preserves its generation capabilities. Video and image generators are showing the same thing on other tasks [5, 6], and we think this points to one model that learns every modality of scene together, and keeps improving with data and compute after task-specific designs have stopped. Depth is the first modality we added; normals, segmentation and multi-view geometry will come next. Limitations. There are several limitations to this approach. Depth is still relative. The prediction is defined up to scale and shift in log space, so Iris-Z gives neither metric distances nor the camera; MoGe3 predicts both. This is the gap we want to close next: we will add one more group of tokens to the same sequence that predicts the camera intrinsics. With the camera known, the depth map becomes point cloud from which the shift can be obtained, so what remains should be single global scale. Resolution and depth range. We train at up to about 10242 pixels and do not evaluate on 2 to 8 MP images (Spring, Synth4K). Cost. Each prediction takes 40 passes of 9B or 32B transformer: about 15 per 5122 image for Iris-Z-big against MoGe-3s 0.41 on the same GPU. We made that trade on purpose. The open question was whether one generative model could match the specialists at all; speed is problem we already know how to solve the same way image generation did. We believe this is the right path, and that the optimisations will follow. Generation drift. Generated images move towards the look of the training data: the human preference score of Iris-Z-big falls from 26.71 to 24.30, prompt adherence drops slightly (CLIP 27.42 against 27.85) and photorealism rises. Single images. We evaluate one image at time; consistency across video frames or views is not measured.
